divert

dy-VURT -- built on the root '-vert-,' meaning to turn. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To divert is to cause something to change course or direction; also, to distract someone's attention.

Construction crews had to divert the river temporarily while they repaired the old bridge.

Worked Example

A birthday clown juggles brightly colored balls and tells jokes to keep a group of restless toddlers entertained while their parents quietly set up the surprise cake in the next room.

That deliberate redirecting of attention, away from its original focus, is exactly what divert means. Unlike 'stop,' which halts something entirely, divert simply redirects it elsewhere.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

reroute: To reroute is to send something along a different planned path -- closed roads reroute traffic, and airlines reroute flights. To divert is broader and often more sudden: you can divert a river, a flight, or someone's attention, with no new route mapped out in advance.

distract: To distract is to pull someone's attention away, usually without offering any particular new focus -- loud noise distracts a student. To divert can do more: it steers the attention, or the river, or the traffic, toward somewhere else in particular.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

maintain: to keep something on its original course

focus: to direct all of one's attention onto one thing

Where it sits · how dramatic the turn feels — redirect → divert → derail

redirect vs. divert: Redirect is a fairly neutral, everyday word -- it just means sending something a new way. Divert can feel slightly more dramatic, often implying an unexpected or urgent change of course.

derail vs. divert: Derail is more extreme than divert: a diverted river or flight is guided onto a new course and keeps going, while a derailed plan or train is knocked off course entirely, with no new path at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — di- (dis-)

prefix — di- (dis-): aside, away (Latin)

root — -vert-

root — -vert-: to turn (Latin (vertere))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin vertere meant 'to turn.' Divert, at its root, means to turn something aside or away -- redirecting its path, whether that path is a river, a road, or someone's attention.

Use the root in a new word: convert

Use the root in a new word: convert: The old warehouse was converted into a series of modern apartments.
